title: The Talented Jerk

scenario.situation: A post-hire review finds that among engineers hired in the last two years, coding-assessment scores and interview-charisma ratings are negatively correlated (r ≈ −0.41). Leadership is alarmed.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The Head of Engineering concludes that truly skilled engineers are just bad at interviews, and wants to drop the charisma-heavy panel interview to stop losing top talent.
scenario.question: Is the negative correlation real — and should Nimbus drop the interview?

decisions.prompt: The Head of Eng wants a quick answer. How do you frame the investigation?

options.label: Deepen the hired-engineers analysis
options.detail: Dig further into the hired cohort — break it down by team, tenure, or hiring manager to explain the negative correlation.
options.consequence: You find the negative correlation holds across teams and managers, which feels conclusive. But every slice still conditions on the same selection event — being hired — so the confound is baked into every cut you make.
options.divergenceCost: Stayed inside the conditioned sample; every additional slice inherits the same selection bias.

options.label: Diagnostic scope expansion — include the full applicant pool
options.detail: Ask whether the pattern exists before the hiring decision. Pull data on all applicants, not just those who were hired, and check the correlation in the full pool.
options.consequence: You immediately have a comparison: the same two scores measured in a population that hasn't been filtered by hiring. Whatever you find there is not contaminated by the selection event, so you can test whether the correlation is a property of people or a property of your hiring filter.

options.label: Survey hired engineers about their interview experience
options.detail: Ask high-coding-skill hires whether they felt disadvantaged by the interview format.
options.consequence: You get rich qualitative feedback, but it still comes entirely from people who passed both filters — you're hearing only from survivors. The correlation question is untouched.
options.divergenceCost: Chose a slow, survivor-biased instrument instead of examining the selection mechanism directly.

options.label: Benchmark against industry interview-design research
options.detail: Pull academic and industry studies on whether technical and interpersonal skills trade off.
options.consequence: External research gives you priors but not an answer about Nimbus specifically. You've deferred rather than investigated, and the Head of Eng still needs a data-backed recommendation about this hiring process.
options.divergenceCost: Substituted generic benchmarks for a diagnosis of Nimbus's own selection process.

decisions.prompt: You now have scores for all applicants. Which view do you trust to test whether the correlation is real?

artifact.title: Avg. charisma rating by coding-score quartile — HIRED engineers only
artifact.caption: Among the 312 hired engineers, average charisma drops as coding score rises — the pattern that alarmed leadership. But this sample excludes everyone who was rejected.

options.label: Correlation of the two scores inside the hired cohort
options.detail: Use the hired-engineers dataset — it's larger, cleaner, and has post-hire performance data too.
options.consequence: The correlation is −0.41 and looks robust at n = 312. But this is exactly the conditioned sample: every person here cleared at least one of the two bars to get hired. The negative correlation could be entirely manufactured by that filter, not by any real trade-off in the population.
options.divergenceCost: Validated the signal inside the biased sample — confirmed an artifact, not a fact.

options.label: Correlation of the two scores across all applicants (full pool)
options.detail: Compute the same correlation on every applicant who completed both assessments, hired or not.
options.consequence: In the full pool of 1,847 applicants the correlation is +0.03 — statistically indistinguishable from zero. The two traits are unrelated in the population. The negative signal in the hired cohort is entirely a product of the hiring filter, not a property of engineers.

artifact.title: Avg. charisma rating by coding-score quartile — ALL applicants (n = 1,847)
artifact.caption: Across the unfiltered applicant pool the relationship is flat. The negative correlation seen in hired engineers disappears entirely once conditioning on hiring is removed.

decisions.prompt: The full-pool correlation is essentially zero. What do you tell the Head of Engineering?

options.label: "Coding skill and charisma are unrelated — keep the interview as-is, problem solved."
options.detail: Declare the negative correlation an artifact and close the case.
options.consequence: You've correctly diagnosed the bias, but 'keep everything as-is' doesn't follow from the data either. The finding reveals that your hiring bar may be excluding candidates who are strong on both dimensions — that's worth a deliberate audit, not a shrug.
options.divergenceCost: Overconcluded from the fix — correct diagnosis, unjustified prescription to do nothing.

options.label: "The negative correlation is a statistical artifact of conditioning on who got hired — not a real trade-off. But this also means our filter may be discarding high-skill, high-charisma candidates. I'd recommend auditing the rejection pool and running a structured review before changing or keeping the interview design."
options.detail: Name the collider bias, correct the misconception, and flag the implication worth investigating.
options.consequence: You've dissolved the false conclusion, given the Head of Eng a precise explanation of why the data was misleading, and opened a productive next question — whether the current hiring bar is optimally placed — without overclaiming what the correlation data alone can prove.

insight: The negative correlation between coding skill and charisma was entirely manufactured by conditioning on a common effect — getting hired. Because Nimbus hires anyone who clears either bar, the hired pool is enriched with people who are high on one dimension but not both, creating a spurious negative relationship that vanishes in the full applicant pool. This is collider bias: when you filter on a variable that is caused by two others, you induce a correlation between those causes that does not exist in the world. The lesson is structural: before trusting any correlation, ask whether your sample was selected on something downstream of the variables you are measuring.
